bridges.description: A contingent universe requires a necessary divine explanation.
Fine-tuning is best explained by design.
Theism grounds moral value, meaning, and purpose.
Appropriately reasoned atheism can constitute knowledge.
Theism is weak against naturalistic background knowledge.
Ordinary causal intuitions may fail at cosmic origin.
Moral judgment need not imply divine grounding.
Reports and ordinary history do not establish miracles.

sections.title: Warrant, proof, and burdens
sections.rationale: Both sides distinguish warrant from conclusive proof and dispute what positive atheism must justify.

sections.title: Contingency and cosmic origin
sections.rationale: The debate centrally contests cosmic explanation and whether ordinary causal principles extend to origins.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and explanatory method
sections.rationale: Craig's design inference meets Kappel's comparative hypothesis standard.

sections.title: Moral grounding, meaning, and importance
sections.rationale: The speakers distinguish moral judgments, metaphysical grounding, and practical consequences.

sections.title: Testimony, resurrection, and religious diversity
sections.rationale: Craig's Christian bridge depends on resurrection testimony that Kappel separates from ordinary history.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Positive atheism needs more than absence of evidence.
moves.warrant: Something may exist without available evidence; absence alone remains compatible with agnosticism.
moves.inference: Kappel's stronger claim needs positive warrant.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete opening burden argument, including multiverse illustration and conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: The absence of evidence for something does not prove
he needs to give us some positive arguments for atheism
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.

burdenContact.rationale: Requires justification for the denial of God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The contingent universe is explained by a necessarily existing unembodied mind.
moves.warrant: The universe could have differed or not existed; abstract objects lack causal power.
moves.inference: A necessary mind is the remaining explanatory candidate Craig identifies with God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete contingency argument and evidence-not-knockdown-proof qualification.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: The universe does not therefore exist necessarily but contingently
abstract objects don't stand in causal relations
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: A principal independent route to the motion.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.warrant: Craig compares necessity, chance, and design, rejecting necessity and chance.
moves.inference: A transcendent designer is inferred as the preferred option.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete fine-tuning case from phenomenon through formal conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: three live explanatory options for this extraordinary fine-tuning
Design then seems to be the best explanation
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: A central inference to the best explanation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Resurrection best explains three asserted historical facts and entails God.
moves.warrant: Craig cites empty tomb, appearances, and transformed disciple belief while rejecting common alternatives.
moves.inference: The claimed historical inference supports Christian theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete opening resurrection case with all three facts and conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: three facts which are recognized by the majority of historians
But that entails that God exists
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.

burdenContact.rationale: Links claimed historical facts to resurrection and God.

moves.speaker: Klemens Kappel
moves.claim: People who reject God for the right reasons can be positioned to know God does not exist.
moves.warrant: Kappel defines the target God and qualifies the claim to appropriately reasoned nonbelievers.
moves.inference: Reasonable atheism may be knowledge rather than mere withholding.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete definition and qualified knowledge thesis with deity analogy.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: those who don't believe that God exists for the right kind of reasons
we are in a position to know that
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.

burdenContact.rationale: Supports the qualified denial of the motion.

moves.speaker: Klemens Kappel
moves.claim: The God hypothesis should be compared with naturalistic background knowledge under ordinary empirical standards.
moves.warrant: Remote alternatives with thin evidence are normally set aside; Kappel explicitly denies inferring nonexistence from bare absence of evidence.
moves.inference: Theism may reasonably be rejected as a weak rival hypothesis without conclusive disproof.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete framework, scientific analogy, and absence-of-evidence qualification.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we should consider the God hypothesis
treating the God hypothesis as we would treat any other hypothesis
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: Kappel's main framework for reasonable atheism.

burdenContact.rationale: Compares theism against empirical background knowledge.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes comparative rejection from bare absence of evidence.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Objective moral values and duties imply God's existence.
moves.warrant: Craig argues naturalism cannot supply objectively binding duties while moral experience apprehends them.
moves.inference: God is inferred as the ground of objective moral values.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete first-rebuttal moral syllogism with both premises and conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God did not exist, objective moral values and duties would not exist
objective moral values and duties do exist
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: A distinct argument for the motion.

moves.speaker: Klemens Kappel
moves.claim: Ordinary causal intuitions may not govern the universe's origin.
moves.warrant: The explanatory principle is disputed and cosmic origin is unlike ordinary events.
moves.inference: Craig cannot simply transfer everyday causal expectations to the Big Bang.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Focused first-rebuttal challenge to the explanatory principle and its cosmic application.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: every contingent entity has an explanation
the creation of the universe was by no means an ordinary event
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: Targets the main pro explanatory premise.

burdenContact.rationale: Limits causal intuitions at cosmic origin.

responseComponents.description: Disputes applying its explanatory principle to the universe.

moves.speaker: Klemens Kappel
moves.claim: Agreement that child abuse is wrong does not settle objective moral properties or divine grounding.
moves.warrant: Kappel distinguishes first-order agreement from metaethical explanation and mentions reason-based alternatives.
moves.inference: Craig's example does not establish the moral argument's metaphysical premises.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete closing clarification of the moral-ontology dispute.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Everyone agrees that abusing a child is wrong
The dispute is whether you need to postulate objective moral values
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.

burdenContact.rationale: Separates moral judgment from divine grounding.

responseComponents.description: Challenges whether the shared wrongness judgment establishes divine grounding.

moves.speaker: Klemens Kappel
moves.claim: Evidence for Jesus and miracle reports is stronger than evidence that divinity or miracles occurred.
moves.warrant: Kappel accepts Jesus' existence and the existence of reports but asks whether another explanation fits them.
moves.inference: Historical persons and reports do not by themselves establish resurrection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Complete late audience answer before the questioner's follow-up, preserving person/report/event distinctions.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the evidence that he was God's son is less solid
the reports are there no doubt
moves.attributionRationale: Formal floor and source boundaries identify the speaker.

responseComponents.description: Separates reports and ordinary history from supernatural occurrence.

majorLines.description: Both openings: burden, contingency, fine-tuning, resurrection, qualified atheism, and naturalistic comparison.
Both rebuttal rounds reviewed; causal-intuition challenge selected, while repeated summaries and subsidiary examples are omitted below.
Both closings reviewed; Kappel's moral-grounding clarification selected, with Craig's repeated summaries accounted for below.
Complete question period reviewed; selected answers cover importance and the history/report/miracle distinction.
